High-frequency data is a different class of problem than ordinary key-value records. Metrics, event streams, sensor readings, and operational telemetry arrive continuously and grow quickly, so the system must optimize not only for correctness but also for ingest rate, compression, retention, and time-window queries. In ThemisDB, the timeseries module handles exactly that challenge.

The general idea is simple: time-series data is usually append-heavy, query-heavy, and retention-sensitive. A good timeseries engine must ingest high-volume points efficiently, compress them without losing analytical fidelity, keep queries fast across time windows, and retain data according to policies that match operational or business needs. ThemisDB builds this into a dedicated module with ingestion, storage, query, retention, downsampling, and compression behavior.

This makes the module highly relevant for monitoring, telemetry, infrastructure intelligence, and operational analytics. It is not just an isolated data structure; it is a core capability for systems that need to observe and reason about events over time. The local documentation in README.md, ARCHITECTURE.md, and the wider platform framing in docs/compendium/docs/index.md all place the module at the intersection of storage, observability, and operational analysis.

The first core capability is high-volume ingestion. Modern telemetry workloads can generate bursts of data that are far beyond what a generic transactional path is designed to handle efficiently. The timeseries layer therefore optimizes how data is written, buffered, and flushed so that write pressure remains manageable without losing accuracy.

The second core capability is efficient compression and storage. Time-series data tends to have repeating patterns and highly structured values, which makes it ideal for compression. ThemisDB uses techniques such as Gorilla-style compression to keep footprint low while maintaining enough fidelity for analytic queries. This matters because storage cost and query performance are tightly coupled in high-frequency systems.

The third core capability is retention and time-window analysis. Data is not kept forever in every workload, and not every query needs the same granularity. The timeseries module supports retention policies, downsampling, aggregation, and efficient time-range lookups so that operators can keep the most important historical signal without exploding cost or query latency.

flowchart LR


A[Raw telemetry] --> B[Ingest + buffer] B --> C[Compression + storage] C --> D[Aggregation / query] D --> E[Retention + downsampling] E --> F[Operator insight]</pre>


For customers and operators, the practical value is clear: better monitoring, shorter diagnostics, and lower cost for high-frequency telemetry or operational time data. A timeseries engine helps teams move from raw event volume to actionable understanding: trends, anomalies, baseline changes, and incident windows all become visible in a structured way. This is especially important for AI-assisted operations, infrastructure monitoring, and large-scale system health analysis.


ThemisDB keeps the boundary precise: the timeseries module owns ingest, compression, retention, aggregation, and query semantics for time-oriented workloads, while lower-level persistence and more general query logic remain in their own modules. That separation is useful because time-series workloads have very different bottlenecks from transactional or graph workloads and deserve a dedicated operational model.

A database can be correct and still be unusable if nobody can explain what is happening under load. Observability is the layer that makes system behavior visible: it explains latency, failure modes, resource pressure, and the internal causes behind slow or unstable workloads. In ThemisDB, observability is therefore not a dashboard accessory; it is part of the platform's operational contract.

The general challenge is simple: once a system runs at production scale, operators need to answer not just whether something is failing, but where it is failing, why it is failing, and what the right intervention path is. ThemisDB addresses this through metrics, tracing, profiling, alerting, log correlation, and diagnostic workflows so that teams can reason about behavior instead of guessing from symptoms. That is the difference between a system that merely runs and a system that remains manageable under stress.

This module is tightly connected to the rest of the platform. It receives signals from storage, query, replication, sharding, security, and AI-related workflows and turns them into operational intelligence. The local module guidance in README.md and the architecture framing in ARCHITECTURE.md make clear that the goal is not only to display values, but to support real diagnosis and response. The same principle is reinforced by the wider systems overview in docs/compendium/docs/index.md.

The first core capability is metrics collection and aggregation. Reliable visibility starts with consistent measurement: request latency, queue pressure, resource consumption, error rates, and process health need to be captured in a standardized, queryable way. Without this, operators cannot distinguish normal variance from the early warning signs of an emerging incident.

The second core capability is distributed tracing and profiling. When a request spans multiple subsystems or a performance hot path emerges, teams need to see where time is spent and where failure boundaries are crossed. Tracing and profiling make that path visible, which is essential in systems that mix query execution, storage access, replication behavior, and AI orchestration in the same workload.

The third core capability is alerting and incident diagnosis. Metrics and traces are only useful when they lead to action. ThemisDB's observability layer supports rule-based alerting and diagnostic workflows so anomalies become actionable signals rather than vague reports. This improves response time, reduces false assumptions during incidents, and supports better SLO adherence in real production environments.

flowchart LR


A[System signals] --> B[Metrics / traces / logs] B --> C[Aggregation and correlation] C --> D[Alerting and diagnosis] D --> E[Operator response and remediation]</pre>


The practical value is substantial. For customers, better observability means lower mean time to resolve issues and fewer surprises during peak load or partially degraded states. For operators, it enables clear diagnosis of whether the problem originates in query execution, storage latency, replication lag, network constraints, or resource saturation. In enterprise deployment terms, that translates directly into higher trust, better uptime, and lower risk when production conditions change.


Observability is also a governance feature. Systems become operable not only when they are fast, but when teams can explain what is happening and where responsibility begins. ThemisDB therefore treats observability as a cross-cutting platform concern, not as a secondary monitoring add-on. It keeps the subsystem bounded: observability owns measurement, anomaly detection, metrics streams, and diagnostic surfaces, while the underlying subsystem logic remains in the owning module. That separation is crucial because the same symptom can be caused by storage, query, replication, or network behavior; visibility works best when ownership and diagnosis remain explicit.

As data volumes grow, a single node or a single storage path becomes the bottleneck. Sharding solves that by partitioning data and workload across multiple nodes so the system can scale horizontally without turning every request into a global bottleneck. In ThemisDB, the sharding module is the part that decides where data lives, how requests are routed, and how the platform behaves when topology changes or a node becomes unavailable.

The general challenge is not only capacity, but controlled scale-out. A distributed database can grow in size without becoming easier to operate if partitions are poorly placed, routing is unstable, or rebalance events create hidden inconsistency. ThemisDB addresses this with routing logic, placement policies, replication coordination, and repair/rebalance behavior so that scale-out remains predictable instead of chaotic. That is what makes sharding a system-level control plane, not just a storage optimization.

This module is central to large-scale deployment patterns. It connects the storage and replication layers to the actual runtime topology and is where a single-node architecture becomes a coherent distributed system. The local contract in README.md and the architecture context in ARCHITECTURE.md make that clear, and the broader systems narrative in docs/compendium/docs/index.md provides useful cross-platform grounding for topology and load behavior.

The first core capability is placement and routing. Requests must be sent to the correct shard based on key, policy, and current topology. This is the most visible sharding feature from a developer and operator perspective, because it determines whether the database remains fast and predictable under load and whether request paths remain stable as the cluster evolves. Without consistent routing, operators cannot reason about capacity or latency in a meaningful way.

The second core capability is controlled rebalancing and repair. Data is not static forever. As nodes are added, removed, or rebalanced, ThemisDB must move data and adjust routing without creating inconsistent behavior or long periods of degraded service. The sharding model therefore includes data migration, repair, and rebalancing logic so that scale changes do not silently undermine correctness or base availability.

The third core capability is distributed coordination and resilience. Sharding is not just about dividing data; it also defines behavior under partial outages, topology drift, or cross-shard transaction requirements. The module includes health checks, routing state awareness, and fail-closed behaviors so degraded or inconsistent states become explicit and diagnosable rather than quietly incorrect.

flowchart LR


A[Request] --> B[Shard router] B --> C[Target partition] C --> D[Local shard execution] D --> E[Replication / repair / rebalance] E --> F[Operator-visible health state]</pre>


For customers and operators, the value is operationally significant: more scale, better workload isolation, and a clearer path to resilience as the system grows. A well-designed sharding strategy helps avoid hotspots, supports larger datasets, and keeps cluster maintenance manageable. It also reduces operational risk by making routing and repair behavior explicit instead of hidden inside ad hoc assumptions. In real deployment settings, this translates into more predictable performance under growth and a lower chance that a topology change creates a user-visible outage.


ThemisDB keeps this boundary clear: sharding owns partitioning, routing, coordination, repair, and topology-aware runtime behavior, while storage, query execution, and network transport remain separate concerns. That separation is important because distributed infrastructure is only manageable when failure domains are visible and responsibility remains explicit. In other words, sharding is not merely a storage layout feature; it is a platform scaling and resilience mechanism.

Availability and correctness are not the same thing. A database can be fast while still failing the moment a node disappears, a region goes offline, or a network partition appears. The replication module is the part of ThemisDB that turns isolated storage into a resilient platform by keeping data synchronized, making failover explicit, and preserving a recoverable view of the system under disruption.

The general challenge is straightforward: if a primary node fails, the system must continue with a clearly defined safety model. ThemisDB addresses this through leader-follower replication, failover orchestration, WAL shipping, conflict handling, and replication observability. These are not just operational niceties; they determine whether the system can recover safely after an outage or continue serving without silent divergence.

In practical terms, replication is about keeping the system honest across multiple nodes. Data moved from primary to replica must preserve ordering, remain recoverable under lag, and remain diagnosable when a replica falls behind. The module-level contract in README.md, the architecture context in ARCHITECTURE.md, and the broader systems view in docs/compendium/docs/index.md all reinforce that this is an availability and correctness concern, not a niche transport topic.

The first core capability is safe data propagation. WAL shipping and replica synchronization ensure that durable changes are not only written locally, but also transmitted in a controlled way to followers or remote sites. This matters because a system that accepts writes without consistent replication is not resilient; it is merely optimistic in the face of failure.

The second core capability is failover and leadership continuity. When a primary is lost or degraded, the system must promote a suitable replica or move to a defined alternative path. That process depends on explicit topology state, health checks, and a deterministic promotion model. Without this, failover becomes guesswork and the system risks split-brain conditions or inconsistent reads.

The third core capability is conflict handling and explainable stream semantics. In distributed systems, update overlap, lag, and topology changes can create ambiguity. ThemisDB addresses this through explicit conflict resolution strategies, logical replication semantics, and observability of lag and health. The goal is not to pretend conflict does not exist, but to make it visible, rule-based, and repairable.

flowchart LR


A[Primary write] --> B[WAL / replication stream] B --> C[Replica catch-up] C --> D[Failover readiness] D --> E[Leader promotion] E --> F[Consistent continuity]</pre>


For customers and operators, the value is mission-critical: better availability, better disaster recovery, and less business risk from outages. A replication layer makes it possible to move from a single-point-of-failure deployment to a platform that remains operational under maintenance events, regional disruption, or partial node failure. It also improves operational trust because lag, topology, and promoted state become visible and can be acted on before the system enters a critical state.


ThemisDB keeps this subsystem properly bounded: replication owns the durability propagation and failover model, while storage, networking, access control, and application logic remain separate concerns. That boundary is essential because reliability problems are easier to fix when the precise failure domain is known. In other words, replication is not only about copying data — it is about preserving continuity and trust under disruption.

A database becomes valuable when it can answer the right questions quickly, predictably, and at scale. In ThemisDB, the query module is the layer that translates user intent into executable work: it parses a request, decides how to access data, combines data models when needed, and returns results under explicit runtime constraints. This is the system boundary where raw storage turns into usable business insight.

The general challenge is not just “can the engine run a query,” but whether it can do so with clear semantics, good performance, and safe operational behavior. ThemisDB addresses this through AQL as a multi-paradigm query language that spans document, graph, vector, geospatial, and timeseries access. The engine normalizes the request, generates an internal execution model, applies optimization heuristics and runtime estimates, and then executes the result path with the most suitable data access strategy. That design is what makes ThemisDB more than a collection of specialized storage backends: it creates a coherent execution layer for hybrid workloads.

This matters because real-world workloads are rarely one-dimensional. Application teams ask for transactional lookups, analytical aggregations, graph traversals, vector-nearest-neighbor searches, and time-window queries in the same platform. If the query layer is weak, then every higher-level feature becomes harder to use and harder to operate. That is why the query module sits at the center of ThemisDB's developer experience and operational model. The local module contract in README.md and ARCHITECTURE.md describes the execution pipeline, while the broader system overview in docs/compendium/docs/index.md helps place query behavior in the wider database architecture.

The first core capability is query interpretation and planning. AQL and structured JSON input are parsed into a normalized representation, transformed into an execution model, and optimized before execution begins. In practical terms, this means the system is not just evaluating a textual request; it is distinguishing intent, data shape, and access cost. This allows the engine to avoid naive scans wherever a more selective path is available and to pick a route that is compatible with filters, cardinality, and runtime state.

The second core capability is multi-model execution. ThemisDB does not limit queries to one access pattern. It supports hybrid execution across document, graph, vector, geospatial, and timeseries data, which makes it useful for real workloads where operational, analytical, and AI-driven questions meet in the same request. This is especially relevant for LLM and retrieval workflows, where semantic search, relationship traversal, and metadata filtering often happen in one integrated query path.

The third core capability is execution control under real load. Cost-based optimization, result streaming, caching, and cancellation semantics allow the system to keep latency and resource utilization predictable. A query is not “fast” only when it succeeds in the happy path; it is also “good” when it remains manageable under concurrency, can be curtailed when its result is no longer relevant, and exposes clear failure behavior when execution becomes invalid or too expensive.

flowchart LR


A[Query request] --> B[Parser / AST] B --> C[Optimization and planning] C --> D[Execution strategy selection] D --> E[Document / graph / vector / spatial / time-series paths] E --> F[Result shaping and streaming] F --> G[User or application response]</pre>


This is where ThemisDB gains a strong product advantage: it supports complex questions without forcing developers into fragmented APIs, while still delivering the predictability needed for production workloads. The query layer improves time-to-insight, reduces operational overhead, and supports workloads that combine transactional lookups, analytical processing, and AI-driven retrieval in one platform. In business terms, that means fewer custom integration layers, better reuse of data assets, and more predictable system behavior under mixed workload pressure.


At the same time, the query engine has a clear responsibility boundary. ThemisDB keeps the module focused on parsing, planning, execution, result shaping, and runtime control, while storage, index management, transport, and topology concerns remain in their own subsystems. This separation is intentional: it makes failure analysis and performance tuning more precise, and it prevents a query issue from being mistaken for storage corruption, network instability, or a topology problem.


The query layer also matters operationally because it is the place where limits become visible. Policies for cancellation, execution budgets, and partial-result behavior are part of the system’s trust model. When a request is too broad, too expensive, or no longer relevant, the engine should fail or stop cleanly rather than degrade silently. That is a core reliability property, not just an optimization nicety.

Storage is the foundation of every durable database. If write durability, crash recovery, or data consistency are weak, every higher layer becomes unreliable. In ThemisDB, the storage module is therefore more than a persistence wrapper: it is the operational backbone for correctness, recovery, and trust.

The general idea is straightforward. Data must be written safely, survive crashes, remain readable in the correct version, and be recoverable to a known point in time. ThemisDB turns this into concrete storage capabilities: MVCC, write-ahead logging, durable replay, backup and point-in-time recovery, and tiered storage policies that move data between hot and cold layers without breaking service semantics. These are not abstract architecture goals; they are the reason production systems can keep running after outages, compaction cycles, or partial failures.

The storage layer is built around the principle that correctness must be explicit. A write is only valuable if it can be recovered reliably, audited cleanly, and interpreted consistently across snapshots. That is why the module includes strict durability and recovery paths alongside the storage APIs in README.md and the architecture guidance in ARCHITECTURE.md. The design is also aligned to the deeper operational background in the storage chapter of the compendium, which explains the RocksDB and LSM foundations behind the runtime behavior.

The first core capability is durable write throughput with explicit recovery semantics. Every committed write is protected by a safe persistence path, and the system can replay or recover the state after restart or partial failure. This is the basis for trustworthy production behavior: users, operators, and downstream services can rely on the database not silently dropping acknowledged writes.

The second core capability is snapshot-safe versioning through MVCC. Instead of overwriting the most recent state in place, the system keeps the necessary version history so readers can see a consistent view while writers continue. This matters for concurrency, analytics, and operational safety, because it prevents torn reads and maintains stable data boundaries during active writes and compaction.

The third core capability is operational recovery and lifecycle control: backups, PITR, compaction, and tiered storage. These features determine whether a system can be restored quickly after corruption, misconfiguration, or an operational error. A storage layer that can restore to a known point in time and move data between layers without violating read guarantees is materially more valuable than one that only stores bytes.

flowchart LR


A[Write request] --> B[Storage API] B --> C[MVCC + WAL] C --> D[Durable commit] D --> E[Snapshot / read consistency] D --> F[Backup + PITR + compaction] E --> G[Service continuity] F --> H[Recovery & restore]</pre>


For customers and operators, this translates into predictable uptime, less risk from crashes, and faster incident containment. A durable storage layer reduces the chance that a restart turns into data loss or inconsistent state, while backups and PITR shrink recovery time to minutes instead of hours. Operationally, it improves system trust: the database remains a reliable substrate for analytics, application data, and AI workloads built on top of it.


ThemisDB makes this explicit in its module boundaries: the storage layer owns persistence integrity, durable lifecycle behavior, and recovery semantics; it does not absorb query planning or network transport concerns, which remain in their own subsystems. That separation keeps responsibilities clear and aligns product promises with implementation reality.

Streaming ist fuer Large Language Models (LLMs) nicht nur ein Komfortmerkmal, sondern ein Kernprinzip fuer nutzbare KI-Interaktion. Die grundsätzliche Idee ist einfach: statt erst am Ende einer langen Generierung die gesamte Antwort zu liefern, werden Token schrittweise ausgegeben. Das verbessert die wahrgenommene Latenz) unmittelbar, macht Teilergebnisse schon während der Berechnung verwertbar und erlaubt eine saubere Kontrolle von Abbruch, Kosten und Betriebsrisiko. In produktiven Systemen ist genau diese Steuerbarkeit entscheidend, weil Antwortzeit, Token-Kosten, Benutzererfahrung und Systemstabilität gleichzeitig beeinflusst werden.

In ThemisDB wird dieses allgemeine Prinzip als plattformweiter Vertragsrahmen konkretisiert. LLM-Laufzeit, Server, Query- und RAG-Orchestrierung sowie die Client-Protokolle teilen dieselben Regeln für Lebenszyklus, Reihenfolge, Fehlerbehandlung und Diagnose. Die Architektur ist damit nicht nur „LLM-geeignet“, sondern in ein umfassenderes System aus Datenfluss, Streaming-Events und Operator-Visibility eingebettet. Das zeigt sich etwa in den AQL- und RAG-Pfaden, die in LLM-Integration beschrieben werden, sowie in den stream-orientierten Real-time-Prinzipien aus CDC- und Event-Semantik. Die Auslieferung selbst erfolgt protokollnah über gRPC-Streaming und Server-Sent Events (SSE), sodass interaktive Antworten über unterschiedliche Client-Arten konsistent steuerbar bleiben.

Das ist in ThemisDB besonders wichtig, weil LLM-Anwendungen selten isoliert laufen. Sie bilden sich meist aus Retrieval, Kontextanreicherung, Prompt-Logik und nachgelagerter Verarbeitung zusammen. Wenn ein Stream ausfällt, kippt nicht nur eine einzelne Antwort, sondern auch die Verbindung von Nutzererwartung, Systemlast und operationaler Diagnose. Deshalb behandelt ThemisDB Streaming als Betriebs- und Qualitätskonzept, nicht nur als UI-Feature.

Die Kernfähigkeit ist ein deterministischer Stream-Lebenszyklus. Jeder Stream wird explizit geöffnet, aktiv betrieben und sauber beendet oder abgebrochen. Das verhindert uneindeutige Zustandswechsel, reduziert race-condition-ähnliche Übergänge und macht Cleanup-Vorgänge reproduzierbar. Die Abbildung zeigt den allgemeinen Ablauf: Start, aktive Auslieferung, kontrollierter Abschluss oder klarer Abbruch.

stateDiagram-v2


[] --> open open --> active: stream_start active --> cancelled: cancel_request active --> closed: finish_reason / eof cancelled --> closed: cleanup_complete closed --> []</pre>


Die zweite Kernfähigkeit ist tokengenaue Auslieferung mit Reihenfolgegarantie pro Stream. Das ist keine rein technische Feinheit, sondern ein Qualitätsmerkmal für verständliche und nachvollziehbare Antworten. Wenn Sequenzen kippen, geraten Kontextaufbau, Zwischenstände und UI-Verhalten auseinander. Deshalb werden Reihenfolgeverletzungen als explizite Fehler behandelt, diagnostiziert und nicht still überdeckt. Diese Logik folgt den gleichen Grundprinzipien wie geordnete Event-Verarbeitung in Change Data Capture- und Event-Sourcing-Systemen.


Die dritte Kernfähigkeit ist kontrolliertes Last- und Fehlerverhalten. Backpressure), Buffer-Grenzen, Disconnects und Cancel-Signale werden als Fail-Closed-Pfade modelliert: Ein Problem führt zu einem klaren Zustand, messbarer Telemetrie und definiertem Cleanup statt zu stiller Degradation. In ThemisDB bedeutet das konkret, dass Stream-Sessions über stream_id operativ nachvollzogen werden und Störbilder über konsistente Signalnamen sichtbar bleiben, etwa [LLM_STREAM:BufferOverflow], [LLM_STREAM:GenerationStall], [LLM_STREAM:BackpressureCascade] oder [LLM_STREAM:TokenOrderViolation] (siehe RUNBOOK_LLM_STREAMING.md). Dadurch können Support- und Plattformteams nicht nur Symptome sehen, sondern Ursachenpfade entlang von Produktion, Transport und Konsument reproduzierbar eingrenzen.


Gerade für RAG-Workflows ist diese Verbindlichkeit zentral, weil Retrieval, Kontextanreicherung und Generierung eng gekoppelt sind und ein Streaming-Fehler unmittelbar die fachliche Verwertbarkeit der Antwort beeinträchtigen kann (vgl. RAG-Ablauf). Stabiler Stream-Vertrag bedeutet hier direkt stabilere Antwortqualität.


flowchart LR


A[Token-Produktion<br/>LLM Runtime] --> B{Backpressure ok?} B -- Ja --> C[Token ausliefern] B -- Nein --> D[Fail-Closed Signal] C --> E{Disconnect/Cancel?} E -- Nein --> F[Naechstes Token] E -- Ja --> G[Idempotentes Cleanup] D --> G G --> H[Diagnose + Telemetrie]</pre>


Für Kundinnen und Kunden entsteht daraus vor allem planbare interaktive KI im Betriebsalltag: Antworten sind früher sichtbar, Sitzungen bleiben auch unter Last steuerbar, und Incident-Situationen können anhand klarer Zustands- und Telemetriesignale schneller eingegrenzt werden. Das verbessert die Time-to-Value in Assistenz-, Analyse- und Support-Szenarien und reduziert zugleich das Risiko schwer reproduzierbarer Live-Probleme in produktionsnahen Umgebungen. Wirtschaftlich bedeutet das kürzere Wartezeiten in nutzerführenden Prozessen, besser kontrollierbare Token-Kosten durch frühe Abbruchfähigkeit und stabilere Service-Qualität bei Lastspitzen.


Gleichzeitig ist die Abgrenzung bewusst transparent: FEATURES.md beschreibt den fachlich-kommunikativen Vertragsrahmen, während normative Implementierungs- und Release-Evidenz in den owning Pfaden und den zugehörigen Governance-Artefakten liegt (insbesondere README.md, ARCHITECTURE.md, ROADMAP.md, PRODUCTION_REQUIREMENTS.md). Diese Trennung sorgt dafür, dass Produktversprechen, technische Nachweise und operative Runbooks konsistent zusammenpassen, statt sich über Dokumentebenen zu widersprechen.

Ueberblick

Implements real-time and batch audio transcription for ThemisDB. Provides a language-agnostic IAudioBackend interface with a production implementation (WhisperPlugin) backed by whisper.cpp and a zero-dependency stub mode for CI environments without a model file. Im Modulkontext werden Aussagen mit Architekturgrenzen, Release-Planung, Produktionsanforderungen abgeglichen. Im Betrieb sind dabei insbesondere Latenz), Observability und Determinismus relevante Qualitaetskriterien. Fuer Querschnittskontext wird das Modul mit den relevanten Stellen im Compendium verknuepft.

Kern-Features im Detail

Die erste Kernfaehigkeit ist IAudioBackend, TranscriptionResult. Das beschreibt einen konkreten, in den Modulquellen referenzierten Verantwortungsbereich.

Die zweite Kernfaehigkeit ist WhisperPlugin (top-level). Dadurch bleiben Integrationspfade zwischen Modulgrenzen reproduzierbar und operativ auswertbar.

Die dritte Kernfaehigkeit ist IWhisperTranscriber, InMemoryWhisperTranscriber. Das unterstuetzt stabile Abnahme- und Aenderungsprozesse entlang der Modul-Roadmap.
